igcse-0580-geometry-plane-figures.description: Read geometric labels and recognise triangles, special quadrilaterals and named polygons.

sections.title: Which point is the vertex of the angle?
sections.label: Read labels and angles
sections.intro: A point marks an exact position. A vertex is a corner where two sides or rays meet. A line segment joins two endpoints.

blocks.html: In \(\angle ABC\), the middle letter B is the vertex. An acute angle is below \(90^\circ\), an obtuse angle is between \(90^\circ\) and \(180^\circ\), and a reflex angle is between \(180^\circ\) and \(360^\circ\). The right angle is \(90^\circ\).

figure.alt: A labelled quadrilateral with vertices A, B, C, D in order.
figure.caption: The middle letter of the angle name identifies its corner.

blocks.title: Read the middle letter of an angle
blocks.prompt: Which point is the vertex of \(\angle BCD\)?
blocks.hint: Find where the two named arms meet.
blocks.solution:
Read the three-letter name in order. The middle letter is C.

The two sides of the angle meet at C.

blocks.html: The first or last letter lies on a ray. It is not the vertex unless it is the middle letter.

blocks.title: Classify an angle by size
blocks.prompt: How is an angle of \(90^\circ\) classified?
blocks.hint: Compare with a quarter-turn and a half-turn first.
blocks.solution:
Compare \(90^\circ\) with \(90^\circ\) and \(180^\circ\).

The angle is right.

blocks.html: Place a small mark at the middle letter before following the rays.

sections.title: How do I tell these triangles and quadrilaterals apart?
sections.label: Look for equal sides and parallel pairs
sections.intro: Check triangle side marks first. An equilateral triangle has three equal sides, an isosceles triangle has at least two, and a scalene triangle has three different sides. A right-angled triangle has one right angle.

blocks.html: Square: four equal sides and four right angles. Rectangle: four right angles. Rhombus: four equal sides. Kite: two pairs of equal adjacent sides. Parallelogram: two pairs of parallel sides. A trapezium has a pair of parallel sides.

blocks.title: Recognise a triangle from its markings
blocks.prompt: Exactly two sides have equal length. Choose the most informative type for the stated property.
blocks.hint: Use the stated equality or right-angle marking.
blocks.solution:
Exactly two sides have equal length.

This identifies the isosceles triangle.

options.A: Isosceles with exactly two equal sides

blocks.html: A square also meets the definitions of rectangle and rhombus. When a question asks for the most specific label, use square.

blocks.title: Distinguish special quadrilaterals
blocks.prompt: Name the most specific quadrilateral with these properties. Four right angles, with adjacent sides of different lengths.
blocks.hint: Use the combination of sides, parallels and angles.
blocks.solution:
The stated property is four right angles, with adjacent sides of different lengths.

These markings describe a rectangle.

blocks.html: Read the symbols for equal sides, parallel sides and right angles before relying on the outline.

sections.title: How do I recognise regular polygons and line relationships?
sections.label: Count sides and identify line properties
sections.intro: Regular means all sides and all angles are equal. A pentagon has 5 sides, a hexagon 6, an octagon 8 and a decagon 10. Interior angles lie inside. An exterior angle is formed at a vertex by extending a side.

blocks.html: Parallel lines in a plane stay the same distance apart. Perpendicular lines meet at a right angle. In Extended vocabulary, a plane is a flat surface and a perpendicular bisector crosses a segment at its midpoint at right angles.

blocks.title: Name a polygon from the number of sides
blocks.prompt: A polygon has 6 equal sides and all its angles are equal. What is its name?
blocks.hint: Decide the side-count name, then whether the polygon is regular.
blocks.solution:
The number of sides is 6, which gives a hexagon.

With equal sides and equal angles, it is regular.

blocks.html: Equal side lengths alone do not make every polygon regular. A rhombus can have two different angles.

blocks.title: Identify line relationships and a plane
blocks.prompt: Which term matches this description? Lines that cross at a right angle.
blocks.hint: Check whether the description mentions staying apart, a right angle, a midpoint or a surface.
blocks.solution: The description matches perpendicular.

blocks.html: Read the word ‘regular’ as two separate tests, about lengths and angles.
A regular polygon has equal sides and equal interior angles. A polygon is irregular if either condition fails.

figure.alt: Two hexagons. The first is regular. The second has sides of unequal lengths.
figure.caption: Both shapes are hexagons. Count the sides to identify the polygon.

blocks.prompt: A five-sided polygon has equal sides but unequal angles. How do you describe it?
blocks.hint: Count the sides, then check both kinds of equality.
blocks.solution: Five sides make a pentagon. Unequal angles make it irregular even though its sides have equal length.

retry.feedback: Five sides make a pentagon. Unequal angles make it irregular even though its sides have equal length.

  1. A
  2. B
  3. C

  2. Isosceles with exactly two equal sides
  3. Scalene with no right angle
  4. Right-angled

Name the most specific quadrilateral with these properties. Four equal sides and four right angles.

  1. Square
  2. Rectangle
  3. Kite
  4. Rhombus
solution: The stated property is four equal sides and four right angles.
These markings describe a square.

examples.title: Name a polygon from the number of sides

  1. Regular pentagon
  2. Regular hexagon
  3. Regular octagon
  4. Regular decagon
solution: The number of sides is 5, which gives a pentagon.
With equal sides and equal angles, it is regular.

examples.title: Identify line relationships and a plane
examples.question:
Which term matches this description? Lines that never meet and stay the same distance apart in a plane.

  1. Parallel
  2. Perpendicular
  3. Perpendicular bisector (Extended)
  4. Plane (Extended)
solution: The description matches parallel.

examples.title: Tell regular from irregular
examples.question: A and B each have six sides. All the sides and angles of A are equal. Figure B has unequal sides. Which is regular?
solution: Both shapes are hexagons. Count the sides to identify the polygon.
A regular polygon has equal sides and equal interior angles. A polygon is irregular if either condition fails.
A is a regular hexagon. B is an irregular hexagon.

extraPractice.hint: Decide the side-count name, then whether the polygon is regular.

extraPractice.solution: The description matches perpendicular bisector (extended).

revision.body:
Read labels and angles

In \(\angle ABC\), the middle letter B is the vertex. An acute angle is below \(90^\circ\), an obtuse angle is between \(90^\circ\) and \(180^\circ\), and a reflex angle is between \(180^\circ\) and \(360^\circ\). The right angle is \(90^\circ\).

Look for equal sides and parallel pairs

Square: four equal sides and four right angles. Rectangle: four right angles. Rhombus: four equal sides. Kite: two pairs of equal adjacent sides. Parallelogram: two pairs of parallel sides. A trapezium has a pair of parallel sides.

Count sides and identify line properties

Parallel lines in a plane stay the same distance apart. Perpendicular lines meet at a right angle. In Extended vocabulary, a plane is a flat surface and a perpendicular bisector crosses a segment at its midpoint at right angles.

Example

\(\angle BCD\) lies at C. A polygon with ten equal sides and equal angles is a regular decagon.

Check yourself

  • Where is the vertex of \(\angle DAB\)?
  • What is the most specific name for a quadrilateral with four equal sides and four right angles?

Answers A and a square.
revision.checks:
• The first or last letter lies on a ray. It is not the vertex unless it is the middle letter.
  • A square also meets the definitions of rectangle and rhombus. When a question asks for the most specific label, use square.
  • Equal side lengths alone do not make every polygon regular. A rhombus can have two different angles.
revision.examTip: Read the word ‘regular’ as two separate tests, about lengths and angles.

igcse-0580-geometry-solids-circle-terms.description: Name solids and distinguish the parts and regions of a circle.

sections.title: Which features identify the solid?
sections.label: Name solids by faces and edges
sections.intro: Compare faces, surfaces and cross-sections. A cube has six square faces. A cuboid has rectangular faces. A prism keeps the same cross-section along its length.

blocks.html: A cylinder has two equal circular ends. A pyramid's triangular faces meet at an apex. A cone has a circular base and an apex. Each boundary point of a sphere is the same distance from its centre.

blocks.title: Identify a solid from its defining features
blocks.prompt: Name a solid with this description. A solid with six rectangular faces whose three dimensions differ.
blocks.hint: Count flat faces and check whether there is an apex or a curved surface.
blocks.solution: Look for the combination of faces and surfaces. The stated features belong to a cuboid.

blocks.html: Only the flat parts are faces in these descriptions. A cylinder or cone also has a curved surface.

blocks.title: Identify a solid from its defining features
blocks.prompt: Name a solid with this description. A polygon base joined to a single apex by triangular faces.
blocks.hint: Count flat faces and check whether there is an apex or a curved surface.
blocks.solution: Look for the combination of faces and surfaces. The stated features belong to a pyramid.

blocks.html: Start by counting matching bases and checking for an apex.

sections.title: Which points does a circle feature join?
sections.label: Identify chords, radius and diameter
sections.intro: The centre is inside. The circumference is the full outer curve. A radius joins the centre to the curve. A chord joins two points on the circumference.

blocks.html: A diameter is a chord passing through the centre. A tangent touches the circle at one point. A semicircle is one half of the circle divided by a diameter.

figure.alt: A circle with centre O and boundary points A, B, C and D. One circle feature is highlighted.
figure.caption: The shaded region reaches the centre along two radii, so it is a sector.

blocks.title: Identify a straight circle feature
blocks.prompt: Name the highlighted straight feature on the circle.
blocks.hint: Check the endpoints and whether the feature passes through the centre.
blocks.solution:
It passes through the centre between two boundary points.

The most specific name is diameter.

blocks.html: An ordinary chord may lie anywhere across a circle. It does not have to pass through the centre.

blocks.title: Distinguish a circle boundary from an enclosed region
blocks.prompt: Name the highlighted feature. For a highlighted piece of the surface, use the name of the enclosed region.
blocks.hint: Ask whether the highlight is a curve, a line, or an enclosed region.
blocks.solution:
The highlighted region is enclosed by two radii and an arc.

This is a sector.

blocks.html: Point to the centre and the two endpoints before choosing the most specific term.

sections.title: What encloses a sector or segment?
sections.label: Separate the curved edge and enclosed parts
sections.intro: An arc is part of the circumference. A sector is enclosed by two radii and an arc. A segment is enclosed by a chord and an arc.

blocks.html: A net is a flat arrangement that folds into a solid. For Extended, the shorter arc between two points is the minor arc and the longer is the major arc, where the lengths differ. A hemisphere is half a sphere. A frustum remains after a smaller similar top is removed parallel to the base.

blocks.title: Use circle vocabulary precisely
blocks.prompt: Which term describes the complete outer edge of the circle?
blocks.hint: The circumference is the full outer curve. Compare a full curve, a part and a region.
blocks.solution: The words identify circumference.

blocks.html: A sector reaches the centre. A minor segment bounded by a chord that misses the centre does not reach the centre.

blocks.title: Name faces, edges, nets and further solids
blocks.prompt: Which term matches this description? A flat part of a solid's surface.
blocks.hint: Decide whether the description is a whole solid, a face, an edge or an unfolded arrangement.
blocks.solution: The defining term is face.

blocks.html: Choose the name by tracing the boundary with your finger.

solution: The defining term is net.

extraPractice.title: Identify a solid from its defining features
extraPractice.prompt: Name a solid with this description. The same triangular cross-section at both ends.
extraPractice.hint: Count flat faces and check whether there is an apex or a curved surface.
extraPractice.solution: Look for the combination of faces and surfaces. The stated features belong to a triangular prism.

extraPractice.title: Identify a solid from its defining features
extraPractice.prompt: Name a solid with this description. One circular base and a curved surface meeting at an apex.
extraPractice.hint: Count flat faces and check whether there is an apex or a curved surface.
extraPractice.solution: Look for the combination of faces and surfaces. The stated features belong to a cone.

extraPractice.title: Identify a straight circle feature
extraPractice.prompt: Name the highlighted straight feature on the circle.
extraPractice.hint: Check the endpoints and whether the feature passes through the centre.
extraPractice.solution:
It joins two points on the circumference without passing through the centre.

The most specific name is chord (not a diameter).

extraPractice.title: Distinguish a circle boundary from an enclosed region
extraPractice.prompt: Name the highlighted feature. For a highlighted piece of the surface, use the name of the enclosed region.
extraPractice.hint: Ask whether the highlight is a curve, a line, or an enclosed region.
extraPractice.solution:
The highlighted region is enclosed by a chord and an arc.

This is a segment.

extraPractice.title: Use circle vocabulary precisely
extraPractice.prompt: Which term describes the longer of two arcs with the same endpoints?
extraPractice.hint: The circumference is the full outer curve. Compare a full curve, a part and a region.
extraPractice.solution: The words identify major arc (extended).

extraPractice.title: Name faces, edges, nets and further solids
extraPractice.prompt: Which term matches this description? A line where two faces of a polyhedron meet.
extraPractice.hint: Decide whether the description is a whole solid, a face, an edge or an unfolded arrangement.
extraPractice.solution: The defining term is edge.

glossary.definition: A flat part of the surface of a solid.
A line where two faces of a polyhedron meet.
Part of a circle's circumference.
Region bounded by two radii and an arc.
Region bounded by a chord and an arc.

revision.body:
Name solids by faces and edges

A cylinder has two equal circular ends. A pyramid's triangular faces meet at an apex. A cone has a circular base and an apex. Each boundary point of a sphere is the same distance from its centre.

Identify chords, radius and diameter

A diameter is a chord passing through the centre. A tangent touches the circle at one point. A semicircle is one half of the circle divided by a diameter.

Separate the curved edge and enclosed parts

A net is a flat arrangement that folds into a solid. For Extended, the shorter arc between two points is the minor arc and the longer is the major arc, where the lengths differ. A hemisphere is half a sphere. A frustum remains after a smaller similar top is removed parallel to the base.

Example

The complete outer curve is the circumference. The straight line through the centre from one edge to the opposite edge is a diameter.

Check yourself

  • Which solid has two matching circles at its ends?
  • Which circle region is bounded by one chord and an arc?

Answers A cylinder and a segment.
revision.checks:
• Only the flat parts are faces in these descriptions. A cylinder or cone also has a curved surface.
  • An ordinary chord may lie anywhere across a circle. It does not have to pass through the centre.
  • A sector reaches the centre. A minor segment bounded by a chord that misses the centre does not reach the centre.
revision.examTip: Choose the name by tracing the boundary with your finger.

igcse-0580-geometry-geometrical-construc.description: Measure and draw lines and angles, and use two compass arcs to construct a triangle from three side lengths.

sections.title: Where do I put the protractor?
sections.label: Align the centre and zero
sections.intro: Place the marked centre of the protractor at the vertex. Align its zero line with the starting arm. Read the scale that starts at zero on that arm.

blocks.html: To draw an angle, mark its value on that same scale. Use a ruler to join the mark to the vertex. To draw a line of a given length, place the ruler zero at the start and mark the required endpoint.

blocks.title: Measure an angle from the correct baseline
blocks.prompt: Measure the marked smaller angle to the nearest degree. Treat the horizontal ray to the right as the starting ray.
blocks.hint: The two scales on a protractor run in opposite directions. Follow the starting zero.
blocks.solution:
Centre the protractor on P. Align the zero line with the ray going right.

Read the scale that starts at zero on that arm. The angle is \(48^\circ\).

blocks.html: Using the opposite protractor scale can swap an acute angle with its supplementary obtuse angle.

blocks.title: Draw an angle from a marked baseline
blocks.prompt: To draw \(68^\circ\) at P, where should the centre of the protractor go?
blocks.hint: Start from the vertex of the angle.
blocks.solution:
Put the protractor's centre at P and align its zero line with the baseline.

Mark \(68^\circ\) on the scale starting on that baseline. Join the mark to P with a ruler.

options.A: At the far end of the base
options.B: At the marked angle on the edge of the protractor

blocks.html: Check whether the drawn angle should be less or greater than a right angle.

sections.title: How do I select both compass radii?
sections.label: Use the two distances to C
sections.intro: Draw AB to its stated length. The third vertex C lies the given distance from A and the given distance from B.

blocks.html: Set the compasses to AC and draw an arc centred at A. Reset to BC and draw an intersecting arc centred at B. Join the crossing to A and B with a ruler.

figure.alt: A triangle is drawn with the three prescribed side lengths. Two compass arcs cross at vertex C.
figure.caption: The arcs whose centres are A and B meet at C. Their radii are lengths AC and BC.

blocks.title: Read a length from a calibrated diagram
blocks.prompt: The reference bar represents 1 cm. Read the length of AB without relying on the size displayed on your screen.
blocks.hint: Compare the length with the marked unit rather than with the size of your screen.
blocks.solution:
There are 4 equal divisions along AB.

Each is the length of the reference bar. The represented length is \(4\,\mathrm{cm}\).

blocks.html: Measuring an angle to guess C does not show that the third side has the stated length.

blocks.title: Use both compass arcs for the third vertex
blocks.prompt: Triangle ABC has \(AB=6\), \(AC=5\) and \(BC=7\) centimetres. With AB drawn, which radius is needed when the compass is centred at A?
blocks.hint: Each arc fixes one distance from an end of the base.
blocks.solution:
Draw AB with length \(6\,\mathrm{cm}\). Use radius \(5\,\mathrm{cm}\) at A and radius \(7\,\mathrm{cm}\) at B.

Their intersection is C. Draw AC and BC with the ruler and keep the arcs.

blocks.html: Keep both compass arcs visible so the construction can be checked.

sections.title: How do I complete a rhombus or check a drawing?
sections.label: Use the arcs on both sides
sections.intro: Start with one diagonal of the rhombus. The other two vertices are each a side length away from both ends of that diagonal.

blocks.html: Leave both arc crossings, one on each side of the diagonal. Joining each crossing to both ends gives four equal sides. Ruler-and-compass constructions show the distances directly.

blocks.title: Use both compass arcs for the third vertex
blocks.prompt: In a ruler-and-compasses SSS construction of ABC with \(AB=6\), \(AC=5\) and \(BC=7\) centimetres, where should C be marked?
blocks.hint: Each arc fixes one distance from an end of the base.
blocks.solution:
Draw AB with length \(6\,\mathrm{cm}\). Use radius \(5\,\mathrm{cm}\) at A and radius \(7\,\mathrm{cm}\) at B.

Their intersection is C. Draw AC and BC with the ruler and keep the arcs.

options.B: At any point on the first arc
options.C: At the crossing of the two required arcs

blocks.html: On a phone, the size of the displayed diagram can change. Use the reference bar when reading a length from a digital diagram and a physical ruler when drawing at a specified length.

blocks.title: Build a rhombus from two compass triangles
blocks.prompt: To construct a rhombus with side \(6\,\mathrm{cm}\) and diagonal \(7\,\mathrm{cm}\), which compass radius is used at both ends of the diagonal?
blocks.hint: Each crossing point must be one side length from both ends.
blocks.solution:
Draw the diagonal as a baseline. Use the side length as the compass radius from both ends.

Use the arc crossing on each side of the diagonal. Join both crossing points to both ends of the diagonal.

blocks.html: Check that the sides and arcs meet at the same labelled points.

solution: Draw AB with length \(5\,\mathrm{cm}\). Use radius \(4\,\mathrm{cm}\) at A and radius \(6\,\mathrm{cm}\) at B.

  2. At the midpoint of AB
  3. At any point on the first arc
solution: Draw AB with length \(5\,\mathrm{cm}\). Use radius \(4\,\mathrm{cm}\) at A and radius \(6\,\mathrm{cm}\) at B.
Their intersection is C. Draw AC and BC with the ruler and keep the arcs.

  3. \(\frac{5}{2}\,\mathrm{cm}\)
solution: Draw the diagonal as a baseline. Use the side length as the compass radius from both ends.
Use the arc crossing on each side of the diagonal. Join both crossing points to both ends of the diagonal.

extraPractice.hint: Each arc fixes one distance from an end of the base.
extraPractice.solution:
Draw AB with length \(7\,\mathrm{cm}\). Use radius \(5\,\mathrm{cm}\) at A and radius \(6\,\mathrm{cm}\) at B.

Their intersection is C. Draw AC and BC with the ruler and keep the arcs.

options.A: At any point on the first arc
options.B: At the crossing of the two required arcs

extraPractice.title: Build a rhombus from two compass triangles
extraPractice.prompt: To construct a rhombus with side \(7\,\mathrm{cm}\) and diagonal \(8\,\mathrm{cm}\), which compass radius is used at both ends of the diagonal?
extraPractice.hint: Each crossing point must be one side length from both ends.
extraPractice.solution:
Draw the diagonal as a baseline. Use the side length as the compass radius from both ends.

Use the arc crossing on each side of the diagonal. Join both crossing points to both ends of the diagonal.

glossary.definition: The starting ray or segment for a measurement.
The distance from the compass point to its pencil.
A visible curve marking positions at one distance from a centre.
A triangle specified by its three side lengths.
A segment joining two vertices that are not next to each other.

revision.body:
Align the centre and zero

To draw an angle, mark its value on that same scale. Use a ruler to join the mark to the vertex. To draw a line of a given length, place the ruler zero at the start and mark the required endpoint.

Use the two distances to C

Set the compasses to AC and draw an arc centred at A. Reset to BC and draw an intersecting arc centred at B. Join the crossing to A and B with a ruler.

Use the arcs on both sides

Leave both arc crossings, one on each side of the diagonal. Joining each crossing to both ends gives four equal sides. Ruler-and-compass constructions show the distances directly.

Example

Draw AB = 6 cm, then use radius 5 cm from A and radius 7 cm from B to locate C.

Check yourself

  • What angle scale starts at the baseline?
  • Which compass radius belongs at A when AC = 4 cm?

Answers The scale starting at zero, and 4 cm.
revision.checks:
• Using the opposite protractor scale can swap an acute angle with its supplementary obtuse angle.
  • Measuring an angle to guess C does not show that the third side has the stated length.
  • On a phone, the size of the displayed diagram can change. Use the reference bar when reading a length from a digital diagram and a physical ruler when drawing at a specified length.
revision.examTip: Check that the sides and arcs meet at the same labelled points.

igcse-0580-geometry-nets-of-solids.description: Match flat arrangements to solids, draw compatible faces and use net measurements to find surface area or volume.

sections.title: How do I predict the folded shape?
sections.label: Count and identify the faces
sections.intro: A cube net has six equal squares. A cuboid net uses three pairs of equal rectangles. Edges that join when folded must have the same length.

blocks.html: For a triangular prism, identify two matching triangle ends and the three rectangular sides. A square-based pyramid has a square base and four triangles that meet at the apex.

figure.alt: A connected flat arrangement of faces folds into a prism.
figure.caption: The two triangular end faces match. The three rectangles join to their three edges.

blocks.title: Match a net to the solid it forms
blocks.prompt: Name the solid formed by folding this net.
blocks.hint: Identify the matching bases or the face that belongs at the apex.
blocks.solution:
There are three pairs of equal rectangular faces.

The folded shape is a cuboid with unequal edges.

blocks.html: Six faces with the right individual shapes can still fold to an overlap if they are arranged badly.

blocks.title: Match a net to the solid it forms
blocks.prompt: Name the solid formed by folding this net.
blocks.hint: Identify the matching bases or the face that belongs at the apex.
blocks.solution:
Two matching triangular bases and three rectangles make the prism.

The folded shape is a triangular prism.

blocks.html: Identify the bases first and imagine turning each attached face through the fold.

sections.title: How do I draw a net that will close?
sections.label: Match every shared edge
sections.intro: Draw one face using the stated lengths. Add the adjacent faces along edges they share. Check each joining length before drawing the next face.

blocks.html: For a rectangular prism, a strip of four side faces can wrap around. Attach the two matching end faces so they close the opposite ends. For a square pyramid, attach one triangle to each side of the square.

blocks.title: Match a net to the solid it forms
blocks.prompt: Name the solid formed by folding this net.
blocks.hint: Identify the matching bases or the face that belongs at the apex.
blocks.solution:
The square is the base, and four triangles meet at the apex.

The folded shape is a square-based pyramid.

blocks.html: The sloping height within a triangular face of a pyramid is not the perpendicular height of the whole pyramid.

blocks.title: Use a cuboid net to get total surface area
blocks.prompt: A cuboid net has three pairs of rectangles. The cuboid dimensions are 4 cm, 3 cm and 5 cm. Find the total surface area.
blocks.hint: Add the six face areas, taking each opposite pair twice.
blocks.solution:
The rectangle areas are \(12\,\mathrm{cm^2}\), \(15\,\mathrm{cm^2}\) and \(20\,\mathrm{cm^2}\). Each occurs twice.

The area of the whole net is \(94\,\mathrm{cm^2}\).

blocks.html: Use a ruler on every straight edge and label the dimensions that carry over when folding.

sections.title: How do I use the measurements from the net?
sections.label: Use all faces for area and one cross-section for volume
sections.intro: Surface area is the sum of the areas of every face on the net. Count all equal copies and keep square units.

blocks.html: For a prism volume, identify one end area and its perpendicular distance from the matching end. Multiply those and report cubic units.

blocks.title: Find volume from a prism net
blocks.prompt: A triangular-prism net has two right-angled triangles with perpendicular sides 3 cm and 4 cm. Each rectangular side is 5 cm along the prism. Find the volume.
blocks.hint: Use one end area and the distance between the two matching ends.
blocks.solution:
The area of each triangular end is \(\frac12\times3\times4\) square centimetres, or \(6\,\mathrm{cm^2}\).

Multiply the end area by the prism length. The volume is \(30\,\mathrm{cm^3}\).

blocks.html: Adding all the face areas gives surface area. It does not give the volume.

blocks.title: Use a pyramid net to add the faces
blocks.prompt: A net consists of a square of side 5 cm and four matching triangles. The perpendicular height of each triangle on its base edge is 6 cm. Find the surface area.
blocks.hint: Use the given height along each triangular face, then include all four triangles and the base.
blocks.solution:
The square has area \(25\,\mathrm{cm^2}\). Each triangle has area \(15\,\mathrm{cm^2}\).

Add the square and four triangular areas to get \(85\,\mathrm{cm^2}\).

blocks.html: Check whether the answer needs square or cubic units before writing it.

examples.title: Match a net to the solid it forms
examples.question:
Name the solid formed by folding this net.

  1. Cube
  2. Cuboid with unequal edges
  3. Triangular prism
  4. Square-based pyramid
solution: Six congruent squares fold to the six faces.
The folded shape is a cube.

solution: The rectangle areas are \(6\,\mathrm{cm^2}\), \(8\,\mathrm{cm^2}\) and \(12\,\mathrm{cm^2}\). Each occurs twice.

examples.question: A triangular-prism net has two right-angled triangles with perpendicular sides 3 cm and 4 cm. Each rectangular side is 4 cm along the prism. Find the volume.
solution: The area of each triangular end is \(\frac12\times3\times4\) square centimetres, or \(6\,\mathrm{cm^2}\).
Multiply the end area by the prism length. The volume is \(24\,\mathrm{cm^3}\).

examples.title: Use a pyramid net to add the faces
examples.question: A net consists of a square of side 4 cm and four matching triangles. The perpendicular height of each triangle on its base edge is 5 cm. Find the surface area.
solution: The square has area \(16\,\mathrm{cm^2}\). Each triangle has area \(10\,\mathrm{cm^2}\).
Add the square and four triangular areas to get \(56\,\mathrm{cm^2}\).

extraPractice.prompt: A net consists of a square of side 6 cm and four matching triangles. The perpendicular height of each triangle on its base edge is 7 cm. Find the surface area.
extraPractice.hint: Use the given height along each triangular face, then include all four triangles and the base.
extraPractice.solution:
The square has area \(36\,\mathrm{cm^2}\). Each triangle has area \(21\,\mathrm{cm^2}\).

Add the square and four triangular areas to get \(120\,\mathrm{cm^2}\).

glossary.definition: A flat layout that folds to make a solid.
A chosen end or supporting face of a solid.
The shape of a flat slice through a solid.
Total area of the external faces and surfaces.
Amount of three-dimensional space inside a solid.

revision.body:
Count and identify the faces

For a triangular prism, identify two matching triangle ends and the three rectangular sides. A square-based pyramid has a square base and four triangles that meet at the apex.

Match every shared edge

For a rectangular prism, a strip of four side faces can wrap around. Attach the two matching end faces so they close the opposite ends. For a square pyramid, attach one triangle to each side of the square.

Use all faces for area and one cross-section for volume

For a prism volume, identify one end area and its perpendicular distance from the matching end. Multiply those and report cubic units.

Example

A triangular prism with end area 6 cm² and length 5 cm has volume 30 cm³.

Check yourself

  • How many triangular ends does a triangular-prism net contain?
  • How many triangular side faces are in a square-pyramid net?

Answers Two, and four.
revision.checks:
• Six faces with the right individual shapes can still fold to an overlap if they are arranged badly.
  • The sloping height within a triangular face of a pyramid is not the perpendicular height of the whole pyramid.
  • Adding all the face areas gives surface area. It does not give the volume.

igcse-0580-geometry-scale-and-bearings.description: Convert drawing distances both ways, measure clockwise from north and plot routes with ruler and protractor.

sections.title: When do I multiply or divide by the scale?
sections.label: Read the distance represented by one unit
sections.intro: A scale connects a drawing length with the real length it represents. Write down what one centimetre represents before starting.

blocks.html: Multiply the drawing length to find the real distance. Divide the real distance to find the length to draw. For a ratio scale, express both lengths in the same unit first.

blocks.title: Convert a scale-drawing length to a real distance
blocks.prompt: A plan uses 1 cm to represent 4 m. A path measures 3 cm on the plan. Find its real length in metres.
blocks.hint: Multiply by the real distance represented by one centimetre.
blocks.solution:
Each of the 3 centimetres stands for 4 metres.

Multiply 3 by 4. The real distance is \(12\,\mathrm{m}\).

blocks.html: A scale of 1 : 500 compares centimetres with centimetres. It does not say one centimetre on the plan stands for 500 metres.

blocks.title: Find the length to draw at the stated scale
blocks.prompt: Draw a line to represent a 12 m path using 1 cm to represent 4 m. What length should the line be?
blocks.hint: Divide the real distance by the distance represented by one centimetre.
blocks.solution:
Share the 12 m into groups representing one centimetre.

Divide by 4. The length to draw is \(3\,\mathrm{cm}\).

blocks.html: Write the unit at each stage. The result for the drawing should be in the unit you can mark with a ruler.

sections.title: Where do I start measuring a bearing?
sections.label: Turn clockwise from north
sections.intro: In ‘B from A’, stand at A. Draw a north arrow at A and measure clockwise to the route AB.

blocks.html: Write the bearing with three digits. North is \(000^\circ\), east \(090^\circ\), south \(180^\circ\) and west \(270^\circ\).

figure.alt: North is indicated by an upward arrow at A. A straight route is shown to B.
figure.caption: The bearing starts at north at A and turns clockwise to the route AB.

blocks.title: Convert the units in a ratio scale
blocks.prompt: A model uses the scale 1 : 400. A real length is 12 m. What is its model length in centimetres?
blocks.hint: Convert the two scales to matching units before dividing.
blocks.solution:
The scale compares the same units. Convert 12 m to 1200 cm.

Divide by 400. The model length is \(3\,\mathrm{cm}\).

blocks.html: The shortest angle from north may go anticlockwise. The bearing still uses the complete clockwise turn.

blocks.title: Measure a three-figure bearing
blocks.prompt: Measure the bearing of B from A. Give a three-figure bearing to the nearest degree.
blocks.hint: Use the clockwise angle from north. A reflex bearing is greater than 180°.
blocks.solution:
Centre the protractor at A and align zero with the north line.

Measure clockwise from north to the ray AB. The reading is \(067^\circ\).

blocks.html: Check whether the bearing belongs in the expected quarter of the compass.

sections.title: How do I draw a route and find its reverse bearing?
sections.label: Combine scale and direction
sections.intro: First convert the real length to the drawing length. Set the protractor centre at the starting point and mark the clockwise angle.

blocks.html: Mark the endpoint along that ray using its scaled distance. To reverse a bearing, add half a turn and subtract \(360^\circ\) if the result reaches a full turn.

blocks.title: Find a reverse bearing
blocks.prompt: The bearing of B from A is \(083^\circ\). Find the bearing of A from B.
blocks.hint: The starting point changes when you reverse the route.
blocks.solution:
The reverse route points in exactly the opposite direction.

Add a half-turn of \(180^\circ\). If needed, subtract a full turn. The bearing is \(263^\circ\).

blocks.html: Swapping the names of the points without changing the measurement leaves the original direction.

blocks.title: Plot a route using length and bearing
blocks.prompt: B is 15 km from A on a bearing of \(067^\circ\). On a 1 cm to 3 km scale, how far from A should B be marked?
blocks.hint: Turn clockwise from the north line at A, then measure the scaled distance.
blocks.solution:
Use the given scale to get \(5\,\mathrm{cm}\).

Place the protractor at A. Turn clockwise from north through \(067^\circ\). Measure the drawing length along that ray.

blocks.html: Show the north line at the point you measure from.

examples.title: Convert a scale-drawing length to a real distance
examples.question: A plan uses 1 cm to represent 3 m. A path measures 2 cm on the plan. Find its real length in metres.
solution: Each of the 2 centimetres stands for 3 metres.
Multiply 2 by 3. The real distance is \(6\,\mathrm{m}\).

examples.title: Find the length to draw at the stated scale
examples.question: Draw a line to represent a 6 m path using 1 cm to represent 3 m. What length should the line be?
solution: Share the 6 m into groups representing one centimetre.
Divide by 3. The length to draw is \(2\,\mathrm{cm}\).

examples.title: Convert the units in a ratio scale
examples.question: A model uses the scale 1 : 300. A real length is 6 m. What is its model length in centimetres?
solution: The scale compares the same units. Convert 6 m to 600 cm.
Divide by 300. The model length is \(2\,\mathrm{cm}\).

examples.title: Measure a three-figure bearing
examples.question: Measure the bearing of B from A. Give a three-figure bearing to the nearest degree.
solution: Centre the protractor at A and align zero with the north line.
Measure clockwise from north to the ray AB. The reading is \(032^\circ\).

examples.title: Find a reverse bearing
examples.question: The bearing of B from A is \(024^\circ\). Find the bearing of A from B.
solution: The reverse route points in exactly the opposite direction.
Add a half-turn of \(180^\circ\). If needed, subtract a full turn. The bearing is \(204^\circ\).

examples.title: Plot a route using length and bearing
examples.question:
B is 8 km from A on a bearing of \(032^\circ\). On a 1 cm to 2 km scale, how far from A should B be marked?

  1. \(4\,\mathrm{cm}\)
  2. \(8\,\mathrm{cm}\)
  3. \(6\,\mathrm{cm}\)
solution: Use the given scale to get \(4\,\mathrm{cm}\).
Place the protractor at A. Turn clockwise from north through \(032^\circ\). Measure the drawing length along that ray.

extraPractice.title: Convert a scale-drawing length to a real distance
extraPractice.prompt: A plan uses 1 cm to represent 5 m. A path measures 4 cm on the plan. Find its real length in metres.
extraPractice.hint: Multiply by the real distance represented by one centimetre.
extraPractice.solution:
Each of the 4 centimetres stands for 5 metres.

Multiply 4 by 5. The real distance is \(20\,\mathrm{m}\).

extraPractice.title: Find the length to draw at the stated scale
extraPractice.prompt: Draw a line to represent a 20 m path using 1 cm to represent 5 m. What length should the line be?
extraPractice.hint: Divide the real distance by the distance represented by one centimetre.
extraPractice.solution:
Share the 20 m into groups representing one centimetre.

Divide by 5. The length to draw is \(4\,\mathrm{cm}\).

extraPractice.title: Convert the units in a ratio scale
extraPractice.prompt: A model uses the scale 1 : 500. A real length is 20 m. What is its model length in centimetres?
extraPractice.hint: Convert the two scales to matching units before dividing.
extraPractice.solution:
The scale compares the same units. Convert 20 m to 2000 cm.

Divide by 500. The model length is \(4\,\mathrm{cm}\).

extraPractice.title: Measure a three-figure bearing
extraPractice.prompt: Measure the bearing of B from A. Give a three-figure bearing to the nearest degree.
extraPractice.hint: Use the clockwise angle from north. A reflex bearing is greater than 180°.
extraPractice.solution:
Centre the protractor at A and align zero with the north line.

Measure clockwise from north to the ray AB. The reading is \(112^\circ\).

extraPractice.title: Find a reverse bearing
extraPractice.prompt: The bearing of B from A is \(154^\circ\). Find the bearing of A from B.
extraPractice.hint: The starting point changes when you reverse the route.
extraPractice.solution:
The reverse route points in exactly the opposite direction.

Add a half-turn of \(180^\circ\). If needed, subtract a full turn. The bearing is \(334^\circ\).

extraPractice.title: Plot a route using length and bearing
extraPractice.prompt: B is 24 km from A on a bearing of \(118^\circ\). On a 1 cm to 4 km scale, how far from A should B be marked?
extraPractice.hint: Turn clockwise from the north line at A, then measure the scaled distance.
extraPractice.solution:
Use the given scale to get \(6\,\mathrm{cm}\).

Place the protractor at A. Turn clockwise from north through \(118^\circ\). Measure the drawing length along that ray.

glossary.definition: The relationship between represented and real lengths.
A clockwise direction from north, given with three digits.
North, east, south or west.
The direction of the same route when travelled the other way.
A diagram segment showing a stated unit length.

revision.body:
Read the distance represented by one unit

Multiply the drawing length to find the real distance. Divide the real distance to find the length to draw. For a ratio scale, express both lengths in the same unit first.

Turn clockwise from north

Write the bearing with three digits. North is \(000^\circ\), east \(090^\circ\), south \(180^\circ\) and west \(270^\circ\).

Combine scale and direction

Mark the endpoint along that ray using its scaled distance. To reverse a bearing, add half a turn and subtract \(360^\circ\) if the result reaches a full turn.

Example

If one centimetre represents 3 km, a route of 15 km is 5 cm on paper.

Check yourself

  • What is the bearing due west?
  • What is the reverse of \(062^\circ\)?

Answers \(270^\circ\) and \(242^\circ\).
revision.checks:
• A scale of 1 : 500 compares centimetres with centimetres. It does not say one centimetre on the plan stands for 500 metres.
  • The shortest angle from north may go anticlockwise. The bearing still uses the complete clockwise turn.
  • Swapping the names of the points without changing the measurement leaves the original direction.
revision.examTip: Show the north line at the point you measure from.

igcse-0580-geometry-similar-lengths.description: Match like sides, choose the direction of the scale factor and find missing lengths.

sections.title: Which sides actually correspond?
sections.label: Match the vertices first
sections.intro: The same angle positions and same relative lengths identify corresponding sides. When names are given in corresponding order, match the first letters, second letters and third letters.

blocks.html: A shape may be turned over or rotated. Follow the same marked angles and endpoints, then pair the sides that join them.

figure.alt: Two similar right-angled triangles. Corresponding corners have matching orientations.
figure.caption: Identify corresponding right angles and pairs of legs before using a length factor.

blocks.title: Match sides using the order of the vertices
blocks.prompt: Triangles ABC and RSP are similar, with vertices in corresponding order. Which side of RSP corresponds to BC?
blocks.hint: Match the two endpoint letters before considering a length.
blocks.solution:
Match each vertex to the letter at the same position in the other name.

The corresponding side is SP.

blocks.html: The leftmost sides on two pictures need not correspond. Check geometric markings or the stated order.

blocks.title: Find the length scale factor in the required direction
blocks.prompt: Corresponding sides of small and large similar shapes are 4 cm and 8 cm. Find the length scale factor from small to large.
blocks.hint: Put the length in the target shape over the matching start length.
blocks.solution:
Put the target length above the starting length. The ratio is \(\frac{8}{4}\)=\(2\).

The factor is greater than one because the target is bigger.

blocks.html: Write the matching vertices in two aligned rows.
Congruent figures have the same shape and the same size. Similar figures have the same shape, with one scale factor for all matching lengths.

figure.alt: Two identical rectangles and a larger rectangle with the same shape.
figure.caption: The three rectangles have the same shape. C has double each length of A and B.

blocks.prompt: Compare a rectangle 4 cm by 10 cm with a rectangle 6 cm by 15 cm.
blocks.hint: Compare the two scale factors for the matching sides.
blocks.solution: Both lengths have been multiplied by \(\tfrac32\). The size changes by that scale factor. The rectangles are similar.

retry.feedback: Both lengths have been multiplied by \(\tfrac32\). The size changes by that scale factor. The rectangles are similar.

sections.title: Which length goes on top of the factor?
sections.label: Divide target by starting length
sections.intro: Use one complete pair of corresponding sides. Take the target length over the starting length.

blocks.html: A factor greater than one gives an enlargement. A factor between zero and one gives a reduction. Apply the same factor to every matching length.

blocks.title: Find a missing length in a larger similar triangle
blocks.prompt: Two similar triangles have corresponding bases 4 cm and 8 cm. A different small side is 6 cm. Find the matching large side.
blocks.hint: Use one pair to find the factor, and apply it to the other pair.
blocks.solution:
The enlargement multiplies lengths by \(2\).

Multiply \(6\) by that factor to get \(12\,\mathrm{cm}\).

blocks.html: Using a ratio of two sides of different types can give a number with no scale-factor meaning.

blocks.title: Find the matching shorter side
blocks.prompt: In two similar triangles the large base is 8 cm and the matching small base is 4 cm. Another large side is 12 cm. Find the matching small side.
blocks.hint: The question goes from the large shape back to the small one.
blocks.solution:
The larger triangle is \(2\) times the smaller one.

Divide the known large side by \(2\). The small side is \(6\,\mathrm{cm}\).

blocks.html: Check whether the target drawing is meant to be larger or smaller.

sections.title: How do I work back to the smaller shape?
sections.label: Keep the direction consistent
sections.intro: A factor describes one direction. If a known factor takes small to large, the inverse goes from large to small.

blocks.html: Divide by the enlargement factor to reverse an enlargement. You can instead multiply by the reciprocal factor. Both approaches use the same matching sides.

blocks.title: Use the same scale factor across a third side
blocks.prompt: Triangles ABC and PQR are similar in that order. AB = 4 cm, PQ = 8 cm and AC = 8 cm. Find PR.
blocks.hint: Read both pairs of letters before calculating the factor.
blocks.solution:
AB corresponds to PQ. The length factor from ABC to PQR is \(2\).

AC corresponds to PR. Multiplying gives \(16\,\mathrm{cm}\).

blocks.html: It is easy to apply the same enlargement factor again when trying to recover an original length.

blocks.title: Use a factor less than one for a reduction
blocks.prompt: A similar drawing is made using a length scale factor \(\frac{4}{5}\). What length in the drawing corresponds to \(25\,\mathrm{cm}\) in the original?
blocks.hint: Apply the factor in the direction stated in the question.
blocks.solution:
This factor is less than one, so the new drawing is smaller.

Multiply the original length by the stated factor to get \(20\,\mathrm{cm}\).

blocks.html: Write ‘from’ and ‘to’ next to each side of the ratio.

examples.title: Match sides using the order of the vertices
examples.question:
Triangles ABC and PQR are similar, with vertices in corresponding order. Which side of PQR corresponds to AC?

  1. PR
  2. PQ
  3. QR
solution: Match each vertex to the letter at the same position in the other name.
The corresponding side is PR.

examples.title: Find the length scale factor in the required direction
examples.question: Corresponding sides of small and large similar shapes are 6 cm and 9 cm. Find the length scale factor from small to large.
solution: Put the target length above the starting length. The ratio is \(\frac{9}{6}\)=\(\frac{3}{2}\).
The factor is greater than one because the target is bigger.

examples.title: Find a missing length in a larger similar triangle
examples.question: Two similar triangles have corresponding bases 6 cm and 9 cm. A different small side is 10 cm. Find the matching large side.
solution: The enlargement multiplies lengths by \(\frac{3}{2}\).
Multiply \(10\) by that factor to get \(15\,\mathrm{cm}\).

examples.title: Find the matching shorter side
examples.question: In two similar triangles the large base is 9 cm and the matching small base is 6 cm. Another large side is 15 cm. Find the matching small side.
solution: The larger triangle is \(\frac{3}{2}\) times the smaller one.
Divide the known large side by \(\frac{3}{2}\). The small side is \(10\,\mathrm{cm}\).

examples.title: Use the same scale factor across a third side
examples.question: Triangles ABC and PQR are similar in that order. AB = 6 cm, PQ = 9 cm and AC = 14 cm. Find PR.
solution: AB corresponds to PQ. The length factor from ABC to PQR is \(\frac{3}{2}\).
AC corresponds to PR. Multiplying gives \(21\,\mathrm{cm}\).

examples.title: Use a factor less than one for a reduction
examples.question: A similar drawing is made using a length scale factor \(\frac{1}{2}\). What length in the drawing corresponds to \(8\,\mathrm{cm}\) in the original?
solution: This factor is less than one, so the new drawing is smaller.
Multiply the original length by the stated factor to get \(4\,\mathrm{cm}\).

examples.title: Compare congruent and similar rectangles
examples.question: Rectangles A and B both measure 6 cm by 4 cm. Rectangle C measures 12 cm by 8 cm. Which pair is congruent, and which pairs are similar?
solution: The three rectangles have the same shape. C has double each length of A and B.
Congruent figures have the same shape and the same size. Similar figures have the same shape, with one scale factor for all matching lengths.

The corresponding side is YX.

extraPractice.title: Find the length scale factor in the required direction
extraPractice.prompt: Corresponding sides of small and large similar shapes are 20 cm and 25 cm. Find the length scale factor from small to large.
extraPractice.hint: Put the length in the target shape over the matching start length.

Put the target length above the starting length. The ratio is \(\frac{25}{20}\)=\(\frac{5}{4}\).

The factor is greater than one because the target is bigger.

extraPractice.title: Find a missing length in a larger similar triangle
extraPractice.prompt: Two similar triangles have corresponding bases 20 cm and 25 cm. A different small side is 28 cm. Find the matching large side.
extraPractice.hint: Use one pair to find the factor, and apply it to the other pair.
extraPractice.solution:
The enlargement multiplies lengths by \(\frac{5}{4}\).

Multiply \(28\) by that factor to get \(35\,\mathrm{cm}\).

extraPractice.title: Find the matching shorter side
extraPractice.prompt: In two similar triangles the large base is 25 cm and the matching small base is 20 cm. Another large side is 35 cm. Find the matching small side.
extraPractice.hint: The question goes from the large shape back to the small one.
extraPractice.solution:
The larger triangle is \(\frac{5}{4}\) times the smaller one.

Divide the known large side by \(\frac{5}{4}\). The small side is \(28\,\mathrm{cm}\).

extraPractice.title: Use the same scale factor across a third side
extraPractice.prompt: Triangles ABC and PQR are similar in that order. AB = 20 cm, PQ = 25 cm and AC = 36 cm. Find PR.
extraPractice.hint: Read both pairs of letters before calculating the factor.
extraPractice.solution:
AB corresponds to PQ. The length factor from ABC to PQR is \(\frac{5}{4}\).

AC corresponds to PR. Multiplying gives \(45\,\mathrm{cm}\).

extraPractice.solution:
This factor is less than one, so the new drawing is smaller.

Multiply the original length by the stated factor to get \(12\,\mathrm{cm}\).

revision.body:
Match the vertices first

A shape may be turned over or rotated. Follow the same marked angles and endpoints, then pair the sides that join them.

Divide target by starting length

A factor greater than one gives an enlargement. A factor between zero and one gives a reduction. Apply the same factor to every matching length.

Keep the direction consistent

Divide by the enlargement factor to reverse an enlargement. You can instead multiply by the reciprocal factor. Both approaches use the same matching sides.

Example

When the base grows from 8 cm to 12 cm, the length factor is \(\frac32\). A matching side of 10 cm then becomes 15 cm.

Check yourself

  • Find the factor from 14 cm to 21 cm.
  • Reverse a factor of 2 to recover the original length corresponding to 18 cm.

Answers \(\frac{3}{2}\) and 9 cm.
revision.checks:
• The leftmost sides on two pictures need not correspond. Check geometric markings or the stated order.
  • Using a ratio of two sides of different types can give a number with no scale-factor meaning.
  • It is easy to apply the same enlargement factor again when trying to recover an original length.

sections.title: When are two matching angles enough?
sections.label: Show correspondence before using the factor
sections.intro: Two matching angle pairs in triangles are enough for similarity. The final pair also matches because every triangle has total interior angle \(180^\circ\).

blocks.html: Give a reason for each pair. A shared angle, a right-angle mark or equal angles in parallel lines can identify correspondence. Two angles establish similarity, but the sizes can differ.

figure.alt: Two similar right-angled triangles. Corresponding corners have matching orientations.
figure.caption: A right angle and one more corresponding angle are enough to establish triangle similarity.

blocks.title: Justify similarity using two angles
blocks.prompt: Each of two triangles has a right angle and an angle of \(42^\circ\). Which fact proves they are similar?
blocks.hint: One common right angle on its own is insufficient.
blocks.solution:
The right angles match and the two angles of \(42^\circ\) match.

Two matching angle pairs establish similarity. The third pair matches from the triangle angle sum.

options.A: Their longest sides are the same length
options.B: Both triangles have the same area
options.C: One pair of corresponding angles is equal

blocks.html: One right angle in each triangle is insufficient. You need a second matching angle or another valid similarity argument.

blocks.title: Find the area after changing the scale
blocks.prompt: Two similar plane shapes have heights \(15\,\mathrm{cm}\) and \(20\,\mathrm{cm}\). The smaller has area \(63\,\mathrm{cm^2}\). Find the area of the larger.
blocks.hint: Identify whether the requested measurement uses two or three dimensions.
blocks.solution:
The length scale factor is \(\frac{4}{3}\).

The area factor is the square of the length factor, giving \(\frac{16}{9}\). Multiply to obtain \(112\,\mathrm{cm^2}\).

blocks.html: List both pairs before using any side ratio.

sections.title: Why is the area factor squared?
sections.label: Multiply both independent lengths
sections.intro: Lengths scale by the same factor in both directions in a similar plane shape.

blocks.html: If lengths scale by \(k\), areas scale by \(k^2\). The surface areas of similar solids obey the same rule because each matching face or patch is two-dimensional.

blocks.title: Recover a length factor from a pair of areas
blocks.prompt: Two similar shapes have areas \(63\,\mathrm{cm^2}\) and \(112\,\mathrm{cm^2}\). Find the length scale factor from smaller to larger.
blocks.hint: The ratio of areas is the square of the ratio of lengths.
blocks.solution:
The area scale factor is \(\frac{16}{9}\).

Take its positive square root to obtain \(\frac{4}{3}\). Lengths are multiplied by the square root of the area factor.

blocks.html: Label the scale ratio as length or area before raising it to a power.

sections.title: How do I find length from a volume comparison?
sections.label: Use the cube and the cube root
sections.intro: Volume changes along three perpendicular directions, all by the same factor.

blocks.html: A length factor \(k\) gives volume factor \(k^3\). To reverse this, divide the volumes to get their factor and take its positive cube root. Then compare corresponding lengths.

blocks.title: Find the volume after changing the scale
blocks.prompt: Two similar solids have heights \(15\,\mathrm{cm}\) and \(20\,\mathrm{cm}\). The smaller has volume \(189\,\mathrm{cm^3}\). Find the volume of the larger.
blocks.hint: Identify whether the requested measurement uses two or three dimensions.
blocks.solution:
The length scale factor is \(\frac{4}{3}\).

The volume factor is the cube of the length factor, giving \(\frac{64}{27}\). Multiply to obtain \(448\,\mathrm{cm^3}\).

blocks.html: Using the square root of a volume ratio would undo only a change in two dimensions.

blocks.title: Recover a linear dimension from two volumes
blocks.prompt: Two similar solids have volumes \(189\,\mathrm{cm^3}\) and \(448\,\mathrm{cm^3}\). The smaller is 15 cm high. Find the height of the larger solid.
blocks.hint: A volume factor changes three perpendicular dimensions.
blocks.solution:
The volume factor is \(\frac{64}{27}\).

Taking its positive cube root gives length factor \(\frac{4}{3}\). Multiply the small height to obtain \(20\,\mathrm{cm}\).

blocks.html: For the same direction, a factor above one must increase lengths, areas and volumes.

sections.title: Which lines reflect the whole shape onto itself?
sections.label: Test a full mirror
sections.intro: Reflecting a shape across a line of symmetry places each vertex, edge and marked feature directly on a matching one.

blocks.html: A non-square rectangle has two lines along its midlines. A square also has two diagonal mirror lines. A usual kite with unequal pairs of sides has one mirror line.

blocks.title: Count mirror lines of a plane shape
blocks.prompt: How many lines of symmetry does the pictured rectangle have?
blocks.hint: Only count lines that put the entire shape into the same position.
blocks.solution:
A flip across a valid line maps every feature to its matching position.

The rectangle shown has 2 lines of symmetry.

blocks.html: A rectangle's diagonal gives two triangles of equal area but does not reflect the rectangle onto itself unless the rectangle is square.

blocks.title: Find the rotational symmetry order
blocks.prompt: Find the order of rotational symmetry of the pictured parallelogram.
blocks.hint: A full turn always returns the shape to its start.
blocks.solution:
Rotate the parallelogram about its centre. Look separately for each exact match during one full turn.

There are 2 matches, counting the full turn once.

blocks.html: Fold along the proposed line and check every corner.

sections.title: How do I count matching positions in a turn?
sections.label: Count the full turn once
sections.intro: The order is the number of matches in one full turn about the centre. Count the return to the starting orientation once.

blocks.html: A regular \(n\)-sided polygon has \(n\) matches. The first positive matching angle is \(\frac{360^\circ}{n}\). A shape with no earlier match has order one.

figure.alt: A regular polygon with 6 equal sides.
figure.caption: The marked line is one mirror of the regular hexagon. Other mirror lines also pass through its centre.

blocks.title: Identify mirror lines of different triangles
blocks.prompt: How many lines of symmetry does this isosceles triangle have?
blocks.hint: The mirror must pair corresponding sides of the same length.
blocks.solution:
Check whether reflecting across a line through a vertex swaps two equal sides.

For the triangle shown, the number of mirror lines is 1.

blocks.html: Count only exact matches of all features. A half-turn does not give the same shape if a decoration or unequal side moves to a different position.

blocks.title: Find the rotational order of a regular polygon
blocks.prompt: Find the order of rotational symmetry of a regular polygon with 6 sides.
blocks.hint: Compare the angle between equivalent vertices with a full turn.
blocks.solution:
A turn to the next vertex is \(60^\circ\). Each of the 6 identical positions gives a match.

The rotational order is 6.

blocks.html: Use the smallest matching positive angle to check your count.

sections.title: How do I complete a mirror pattern accurately?
sections.label: Compare perpendicular distances
sections.intro: On a grid, find the nearest point on the mirror to each shaded cell. Copy the cell to the other side at the same distance.

blocks.html: With a vertical mirror, both copies stay in the same row. With a horizontal mirror, both stay in the same column.

blocks.title: Find the smallest positive matching turn
blocks.prompt: By what smallest positive angle does a regular 6-sided polygon rotate onto itself?
blocks.hint: Divide one turn into equal steps between matching positions.
blocks.solution:
There are 6 equally spaced matches during a full turn.

Divide \(360^\circ\) by 6, giving \(60^\circ\).

blocks.html: Translating a cell by a fixed number of spaces does not reflect cells whose distances from the mirror differ.

blocks.title: Complete a reflection in a mirror line
blocks.prompt: When reflecting a square across the drawn vertical line, what must stay the same?
blocks.hint: Count squares straight across from the vertical mirror, one row at a time.
blocks.solution:
Copy each shaded square to the other side at the same perpendicular distance from the dashed line.

Reflection in a vertical line keeps each row fixed. Fill every matching cell.

options.A: Its column and side of the mirror
options.B: Its distance to the top edge only
options.C: Its row and perpendicular distance from the mirror

igcse-0580-geometry-solid-symmetry.description: Identify symmetry planes and rotation axes of prisms, cylinders, pyramids and cones.

sections.title: Which plane can swap a prism's two ends?
sections.label: Find matching cross-sections
sections.intro: Every right prism has a plane halfway between its two matching ends and parallel to them. Reflection in this plane swaps the ends.

blocks.html: If an end cross-section has a mirror line, extending that line along the length can give another mirror plane. A cuboid with three different edge lengths has three central planes parallel to its faces.

blocks.title: Identify a solid's symmetry feature
blocks.prompt: Consider a right triangular prism with its two ends 6 cm apart. How far from one end is the mirror plane which swaps the matching ends?
blocks.hint: Imagine reflecting the whole solid or rotating it about the named line.
blocks.solution:
The central transverse plane is halfway between the identical ends. Their points match at equal distances across it.

The symmetry must match the entire solid, not just its outline from one view.

blocks.html: A prism's end face is not itself a mirror plane. The solid would reflect outside its original position.

blocks.title: Identify a solid's symmetry feature
blocks.prompt: Consider a cuboid with the three different edge lengths 6 cm, 8 cm and 10 cm. How many mirror planes are parallel to its faces?
blocks.hint: Imagine reflecting the whole solid or rotating it about the named line.
blocks.solution:
Each pair of opposite faces has one central mirror plane between them.

The symmetry must match the entire solid, not just its outline from one view.

blocks.html: Check equal distances to both ends before naming the plane.

sections.title: Which planes and axes fit a circular solid?
sections.label: Use circular cross-sections
sections.intro: A right cylinder has a central lengthways axis through the centres of its circular ends. A mirror plane containing that axis can cut each circular cross-section along a diameter.

blocks.html: A right cone also has mirror planes containing its axis through the apex and base centre. Unlike a cylinder, it has no mirror plane parallel to the base that swaps its top and bottom.

figure.alt: A cylinder shown in perspective. A central symmetry feature is highlighted.
figure.caption: The mid-plane perpendicular to the axis swaps the identical ends. The dashed line marks the central axis.

blocks.title: Identify a solid's symmetry feature
blocks.prompt: Consider a right circular cylinder of height 6 cm. How far from the base is the mirror plane that swaps the two circular ends?
blocks.hint: Imagine reflecting the whole solid or rotating it about the named line.
blocks.solution:
The two end circles lie on opposite sides of the central plane, at equal perpendicular distances.

The symmetry must match the entire solid, not just its outline from one view.

blocks.html: A circular-looking cross-section does not mean reflection across any horizontal slice will preserve the whole solid.

blocks.title: Identify a solid's symmetry feature
blocks.prompt: Consider a right circular cone with perpendicular height 6 cm. How long is the portion of its central symmetry axis from the base to the apex?
blocks.hint: Imagine reflecting the whole solid or rotating it about the named line.
blocks.solution:
The central axis joins the centre of the base to the apex. It is perpendicular to the base, so the part inside the cone has length equal to the perpendicular height.

The symmetry must match the entire solid, not just its outline from one view.

blocks.html: Decide first whether the shape has two matching ends or a single apex.

sections.title: What creates repeating turns of a pyramid?
sections.label: Rotate about the line through its apex and base centre
sections.intro: For a right square-based pyramid, rotate the vertical line through the apex and centre of the base. The square and its triangular faces match every quarter-turn.

blocks.html: The central vertical line of a right circular cone has a match at every rotation angle. For the square pyramid, four specific rotations match during a complete turn.

blocks.title: Identify a solid's symmetry feature
blocks.prompt: Consider a right square-based pyramid whose square has side 5 cm. A turn of \(180^\circ\) about the line through its apex and base centre returns it to an identical position. What is its complete order of rotation?
blocks.hint: Imagine reflecting the whole solid or rotating it about the named line.
blocks.solution:
Viewed down that axis, a quarter-turn matches the base and each triangular face with the next one. There are four matches in one full turn.

The symmetry must match the entire solid, not just its outline from one view.

blocks.html: A central line does not make every angular rotation a symmetry. Check the shape of the cross-section.

blocks.title: Identify a solid's symmetry feature
blocks.prompt: Consider a right circular cylinder of radius 6 cm. Does every plane passing through the central lengthways axis reflect the cylinder onto itself?
blocks.hint: Imagine reflecting the whole solid or rotating it about the named line.
blocks.solution:
Every slice perpendicular to that axis is a circle. Any diameter through its centre is a mirror line of that circle.

The symmetry must match the entire solid, not just its outline from one view.

options.A: Only planes parallel to the circular ends
options.B: No, a curved surface rules out mirror symmetry

blocks.html: Imagine looking down the axis and trace what happens to one corner or face.

examples.title: Identify a solid's symmetry feature
examples.question:
Consider a right triangular prism with its two ends 5 cm apart. How far from one end is the mirror plane which swaps the matching ends?

  1. \(\frac{5}{2}\,\mathrm{cm}\)
  2. \(5\,\mathrm{cm}\)
  3. \(0\,\mathrm{cm}\)
solution: The central transverse plane is halfway between the identical ends. Their points match at equal distances across it.
The symmetry must match the entire solid, not just its outline from one view.

examples.title: Identify a solid's symmetry feature
examples.question:
Consider a cuboid with the three different edge lengths 5 cm, 7 cm and 9 cm. How many mirror planes are parallel to its faces?

  1. 3
  2. 2
  3. 6
solution: Each pair of opposite faces has one central mirror plane between them.
The symmetry must match the entire solid, not just its outline from one view.

examples.title: Identify a solid's symmetry feature
examples.question:
Consider a right circular cylinder of height 5 cm. How far from the base is the mirror plane that swaps the two circular ends?

  1. \(\frac{5}{2}\,\mathrm{cm}\)
  2. \(\frac{5}{3}\,\mathrm{cm}\)
  3. \(5\,\mathrm{cm}\)
solution: The two end circles lie on opposite sides of the central plane, at equal perpendicular distances.
The symmetry must match the entire solid, not just its outline from one view.

examples.title: Identify a solid's symmetry feature
examples.question:
Consider a right circular cone with perpendicular height 5 cm. How long is the portion of its central symmetry axis from the base to the apex?

  1. \(5\,\mathrm{cm}\)
  2. \(\frac{5}{2}\,\mathrm{cm}\)
  3. \(10\,\mathrm{cm}\)
solution: The central axis joins the centre of the base to the apex. It is perpendicular to the base, so the part inside the cone has length equal to the perpendicular height.
The symmetry must match the entire solid, not just its outline from one view.

glossary.definition: A plane reflecting a whole solid onto itself.
A line around which a solid rotates.
A prism with lateral edges perpendicular to its two ends.
The pointed vertex above a base.
A plane cutting across the length of a solid.

revision.body:
Find matching cross-sections

If an end cross-section has a mirror line, extending that line along the length can give another mirror plane. A cuboid with three different edge lengths has three central planes parallel to its faces.

Use circular cross-sections

A right cone also has mirror planes containing its axis through the apex and base centre. Unlike a cylinder, it has no mirror plane parallel to the base that swaps its top and bottom.

Rotate about the line through its apex and base centre

The central vertical line of a right circular cone has a match at every rotation angle. For the square pyramid, four specific rotations match during a complete turn.

Example

A right square-based pyramid matches after 90°, 180°, 270° and 360° about the apex-to-centre axis.

Check yourself

  • Which plane swaps the ends of a cylinder?
  • What joins the cone's apex to the centre of its base?

Answers The middle plane parallel to the ends, and its axis of rotation.
revision.checks:
• A prism's end face is not itself a mirror plane. The solid would reflect outside its original position.
  • A circular-looking cross-section does not mean reflection across any horizontal slice will preserve the whole solid.
  • A central line does not make every angular rotation a symmetry. Check the shape of the cross-section.

igcse-0580-geometry-angle-facts.description: Choose the correct sum or equality and give geometrical reasons for unknown angles.

sections.title: Is this a straight line or a full turn?
sections.label: Recognise the total around the vertex
sections.intro: All the angles around a point make a complete turn of \(360^\circ\). Angles that fill one side of a straight line make a half-turn of \(180^\circ\).

blocks.html: Identify the whole group first. Subtract every known part from its correct total. A missing reflex angle is the remaining large part of the full turn.

blocks.title: Apply the correct line or point angle fact
blocks.prompt: The horizontal line is straight. Find x.
blocks.hint: Decide whether the given angles make a half-turn, a full turn or a vertically opposite pair.
blocks.solution:
Angles on a straight line sum to 180°.

\(180^\circ-48^\circ=132^\circ\).

blocks.html: A straight line through a point does not always make \(180^\circ\) the total for every marked angle.

blocks.title: Apply the correct line or point angle fact
blocks.prompt: The angles shown make one full turn. Find the reflex angle x.
blocks.hint: Decide whether the given angles make a half-turn, a full turn or a vertically opposite pair.
blocks.solution:
Angles around a point sum to 360°.

\(360^\circ-48^\circ-100^\circ=212^\circ\).

blocks.html: Trace a complete half-turn or full turn before subtracting.

sections.title: When are angles equal instead of supplementary?
sections.label: Use crossing lines and triangular interiors
sections.intro: When two straight lines cross, opposite angles have equal size. Adjacent angles on the same straight line are supplementary.

blocks.html: The three interior angles of a triangle add to \(180^\circ\). If one is missing, subtract the other two from that total.

figure.alt: Two straight lines cross. The marked angles are vertically opposite.
figure.caption: The two equal angles lie across the intersection of the straight lines.

blocks.title: Apply the correct line or point angle fact
blocks.prompt: The two intersecting lines are straight. Find x.
blocks.hint: Decide whether the given angles make a half-turn, a full turn or a vertically opposite pair.
blocks.solution:
Vertically opposite angles are equal.

\(x=48^\circ\).

blocks.html: Vertically opposite angles sit across the intersection. They do not share an arm.

blocks.title: Use the angle sum of a triangle
blocks.prompt: In triangle ABC, \(\angle BAC\) is \(48^\circ\) and \(\angle ABC\) is \(54^\circ\). Find \(\angle BCA\).
blocks.hint: The middle letter tells you which corner each angle is at.
blocks.solution:
The three interior angles of a triangle sum to 180°.

\(180^\circ-48^\circ-54^\circ=78^\circ\).

blocks.html: Name the exact geometric fact that justifies each line of working.

sections.title: How do equal sides and diagonals help?
sections.label: Use equal base angles and two triangles
sections.intro: Two equal sides of an isosceles triangle face equal angles. Mark the equal sides and then check which vertices lie opposite them.

blocks.html: A diagonal splits a convex quadrilateral into two triangles. Its four interior angles therefore sum to \(360^\circ\).

blocks.title: Find a base angle in an isosceles triangle
blocks.prompt: Triangle ABC has AB = AC and \(\angle BAC\) = \(42^\circ\). Find \(\angle ABC\).
blocks.hint: Find which angles are opposite the equal sides.
blocks.solution:
The base angles opposite the two equal sides are equal.

Subtract \(42^\circ\) from \(180^\circ\) and share the result equally to obtain \(69^\circ\).

blocks.html: The angle between the equal sides is the apex angle. The equal angles are at the other two vertices.

blocks.title: Find the fourth angle of a quadrilateral
blocks.prompt: Three interior angles of quadrilateral ABCD are \(77^\circ\), \(93^\circ\) and \(114^\circ\). Find the remaining interior angle.
blocks.hint: A diagonal divides a quadrilateral into two triangles.
blocks.solution:
The interior angles of a quadrilateral sum to 360°.

Subtract the three given angles from \(360^\circ\) to obtain \(76^\circ\).
